caseno: First Miscellaneous Appeal No.135 of 2001 with Civil Rule No.384 (FM)/2001
lawyer:
Nazibur Rahman, Advocate ----- For the Appellant. 
Shafique Ahmed, Advocate ----- For the Respondents.
parties:
Shah Alam (Md) ----- Appellant
Vs 
Md Shahidur Rahman and others  ----- Respondents
full_judgment:
Sheikh Rezowan Ali, J: This First Miscellaneous Appeal is directed against the judgment and order dated 28-2-2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Rangpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 1995 (a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act) disallowing the pre-emption.

2. Facts relevant for the purpose of disposal of this appellant, in short, are that 0.0913 acre of land appertaining to plot No. 4376 of CS Khatian No. 883 and 0.1087 acre of land appertaining to plot No of CS khatian No.881 (both the khatians now corresponding to RS khatian No. 757), containing 0.20 acre of land of mouja Radhaballav, police station and district Rangpur (as described in the schedule Ka of the pre-emption petition) belonged to one Hafez Mohammad Hossain Sowdagar who died leaving opposite party Nos. 2-10 as his heirs and heiresses. Subsequently, opposite party Nos. 5 and 6 transferred 0.0833 acre of land to the pre- emptor petitioner Shah Alam by a registered kabala dated 16-4-1992 whereby he became a co-sharer to the pre-emption petition Ka schedule land. Later, opposite party Nos. 2 and 3 transferred the case land, 0.0467 in area, as described in the schedule Kha of the pre-emption petition to the pre-emptee opposite party No.1 by a kabala dated 23-11-1994 beyond the knowledge of the pre-emptor petitioner and without service of notice upon him. Under the circumstances he sought pre-emption of the case land under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

3. Pre-emptee opposite party No.1 contested the case by filing a written objection contending, inter alia, that the pre-emptor petitioner was not a co-sharer in the case land inasmuch as pursuant to his purchase of 0.0833 acre of land from opposite party Nos. 5 and 6 in the year 1992 he got his name mutated in respect of the said land vide Mutation Case No.1354/1992-1993 and thereby ceased to be a co-sharer in respect of the case land. He had thus no locus standi to pre-empt the case land.

4. During the course of trial pre-emptor petitioner examined 3 witnesses while the contesting pre-emptee opposite party No.1 examined 4 witnesses.

5. It deserves mention here that earlier by a judgment and order dated 26-2-1997 learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Rangpur disallowed pre-emption in the instant Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 1995. Being aggrieved the pre-emptor petitioner preferred First Miscellaneous Appeal No.121 of 1997 which was heard by this Court. It was categorically contended by the petitioner therein that he. did not ever submit any petition seeking mutation of the land purchased by him from the opposite party Nos. 5 and 6 in 1992 and that all the papers that came before the court below in that connection were fabricated. It then appeared to this Court that the proceeding record of the said mutation case was not produced before the court below for considering its legality, regularity or otherwise. In order to dispel doubt about it this Court sent the case on remand to the court below asking it to cause production of the mutation case record before it and determine the said allegation raised by the petitioner appellant. The learned court below was also instructed to dispose of the case within 3 months from the date of receipt of judgment and order of this Court. Learned Judge, it appears, made a persistent endeavour to cause production of the said case record before him but it did not come. Concerned Assistant Commissioner (Land) reported that the said mutation proceeding record was not available on search and might have gone missing at the time of shifting of his earlier office from Sadar Upazilla premises to its new premises. However, the learned Judge by placing full reliance upon the Mutation Register (Exhibit- Gha), 2 Rent Collection Registers (exhibit Uma, Uma-(1), Duplicate Carbon Receipt Book (exhibit Cha) showing realisation of mutation fees, etc and Rent Receipt Book (exhibit Chha) found that such mutation did, indeed, take place and that the petitioner thereby ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land. He had, therefore, no locus standi to claim pre-emption under section 24 of the Non- Agricultural Tenancy Act. Accordingly, the learned Judge disallowed the pre-emption petition.

6. Being aggrieved by the impugned judgment and order of the court below dated 28-2-2001 the pre-emptor petitioner has preferred the instant appeal.

<u>7. Mr. Nazibur Rahman, learned Advocate for the petitioner-appellant, has repeated the selfsame argument as he did earlier by pointing out before this Court that the proceeding record of the mutation case having not been produced before the court below it could be presumed that no genuine mutation did, indeed, take place and that all those registers and receipt books produced in support of such mutation were wholly unreliable and the learned Judge should not have relied upon those documents and disallowed the pre-emption petition. Further, according to him, original co-sharership in the land does not extinguish without a partition being made in pursuance of a final decree passed in a regularly constituted suit for partition and, therefore, the petitioner appellant did not cease to be a co-sharer in the case land in absence of such partition and lose his right of pre-emption. To illustrate his submission he has cited a decision in the case of Md Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md Abdul Karim and others reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41.</u>

<u>8. Mr Shafique Ahmed, learned Advocate for the pre-emptee respondent, on the other hand, has submitted that mutation related receipt books and register produced in the court below were genuine documents and were sufficiently indicative of a mutation having taken place in the name of the petitioner-appellant thereby extinguishing his former co-shareship and divesting him of his right of pre-emption of the case land. It was, therefore, hardly of any substance, he submits, if the mutation case record did not come up before the court because of its having gone missing at the time of shifting of the office of the Assistant Commissioner (Land) as reported by the concerned Assistant Commissioner duly endorsed by the Additional Deputy Commissioner (Revenue), Rangpur. According to him, learned Judge thus correctly held that his co-sharership in the case land having extinguished earlier he had no locus standi to claim pre-emption of the said land. In order to substantiate his submission that splitting up of jama extinguishes original co-sharership he has cited a decision in the case of Sunil Krishna Banik and others vs Kailas Chandra Saha and others reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 243 = 36 DLR (AD) 220.</u>

9. We have perused the materials on record and have also given our anxious consideration to the submissions made by the learned Advocates for both the sides.

10. By now it is well-settled that for the purpose of pre-emption under section 24(1) of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act co-sharership in the land' is material. A co-sharer in the land becomes entitled to pre-empt under section 24(1) of the Act if any portion of such land is transferred to a stranger. A pertinent question, however, involved in the instant appeal, is whether the petitioner-appellant, who became a co-sharer in the case land by purchase of a portion thereof earlier, ceased to be a co-sharer therein by getting his portion separated through a mutation proceeding opening a separate jama in his name and whether his co-sharership in the land could not be treated to have ceased without partition of his portion by a final decree passed in a regularly constituted suit for partition.

<u>11. The decision in the case of Sunil Krishna Banik and others vs Kailash Chandra Saha and others reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 243, which related to a proceeding under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, reveals that in the trial Court the pre-emptees raised a plea of disability of the pre-emptor to pre-empt the case land on the ground of his having lost his co-sharership in the holding by separation of his jama through a mutation proceeding. In support of such separation the pre-emptees produced two rent receipts, two municipal tax receipts and another document (not specified) which were received by the trial Court as exhibits A, A (1), B, B (1) and C respectively but the learned Judge declined to consider them in his judgment because of their belated production and eventually allowed pre-emption. Being aggrieved the pre-emptees preferred an appeal before the High Court Division and during the pendency of the appeal filed an application under Order XLI, rule 27 of the Code of Civil Procedure by annexing certified copies of application for separation of old jama which initiated two mutation proceedings, orders passed in the said mutation proceedings separating the old holding and two newly opened khatians as annexures A, A (1), B, B(1) and C, C(1) respectively and prayed for receiving the said documents as additional evidence regarding separation of the said jama. But the appellate High Court Division refused to receive them, as such, and dismissed the appeal. On appeal, their Lordships of the Appellate Division observed" the evidence offered by the appellants to prove that the respondent was no longer a co-sharer was already produced before the trial Court, but this was done only at a late stage of the trial. The evidence was not considered by the trial Court for this reason. It was not produced for the first time before the appellate Court. On the other hand, the exhibits referred to in their application for additional evidence could, if considered according to the appellants, have shown that the respondents had ceased to be co-sharers, particularly when the necessary issue to determine this point was already framed by the trial Court. "With the aforesaid observation their Lordships allowed the appeal and sent the case on remand to the High Court Division for disposal in accordance with law. The aforesaid observation by their Lordships left a clear indication that a co-sharer loses his co-sharership in the tenancy or holding by separating his jama through a mutation proceeding and cannot apply for pre-emption.</u>

<u>12. In the aforesaid decision reported in BCR 1984 (AD) 243 reference was also made to another decision in the case of Md Mafizuddin Patwari vs Abdul Hakim Miazi reported in 33 DLR (AD) 305 wherein it was held that an original co-sharer who ceased to be a co-sharer of the jama cannot apply for pre-emption. It was further held that a co-sharer seeking pre-emption must have a subsisting interest in the holding at the time when he files an application for pre-emption and must continue to hold such interest until the case is finally disposed. It will not be out of place to mention here that separation of jama or sub-division of a holding or tenancy distributing rent whether in the case of agricultural land under State Acquisition and Tenancy Act or in the case of non-agricultural land under Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act, takes place under section 117(1)(c) of State Acquisition and Tenancy Act and the original co-sharers on such separation cease to be co-sharers as such and cannot apply for pre-emption on the ground of co-sharership. The principle is equally applicable in both the cases of agricultural and non-agricultural land.</u>

<u>13. Mr Nazibur Rahman, learned Advocate for the appellant, has, however, drawn our attention, as stated earlier, to a decision in the case of Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md. Abdul Karim reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41 wherein it has been enunciated by their Lordships in the concluding paragraph passing of the final decree in a partition suit finally determines the rights of the co-sharers in the land. Hence, the application for the pre-emptor respondents on the basis of co-sharership is not maintainable." Supporting the above view learned Advocate for the appellant has tried to impress upon us that a co-sharer does not cease to be a co-sharer in the land forfeiting his right of pre-emption until his portion has been partitioned by a decree passed in a regularly constituted partition suit and that separation of jam a has nothing to do with termination of his co-sharership debarring him of his right of pre-emption. But a contrary view has been expressed in a decision in the case of SM Basiruddin vs Zahurul Islam Chowdhury and another reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 wherein it has been held by their Lordships of the Appellate Division, "Partition of the land amongst co-sharers on the basis of Civil Court decree does not bring about the division of the tenancy having the same jama." Consequently, we find, co-sharership in the land does not terminate on partition and right of pre-emption is not lost unless the jama has been split up in accordance with law. Placing reliance upon the said decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 a Division Bench of this court in its decision in the case of SM Nasirul Haque vs Omar Faruque Chowdhury and others, reported in 7 MLR 46 = 54 DLR 181, reiterated, "A final decree passed in a partition suit or amicable partition though separates and divides the land for the purpose of possession but does not ipso facto terminate co-ownership in such land till subdivision of the holding and distribution of rents takes place only in accordance with law." In our natural anxiety to be cautious in dispensing justice we have meticulously found that the decision reported in 35 DLR (AD) 230 was not brought to the notice of their Lordships when they were pronouncing the decision in the case of Shafiuddin Chowdhury vs Md. Abdul Karim reported in 52 DLR (AD) 41 propagating forfeiture of right of pre-emption on account of a final decree being passed in a suit for partition extinguishing co-sharership in the land. It does not also appear to us that their Lordships expressed any disapproval of separation of jama as a recognised form of extinction of co-sharership in the land debarring right of pre-emption. So, in our view, separation of jama also terminates co- sharership.</u>

14. Now let us consider if, on the basis of the materials and evidence on record, learned court below correctly held that the petitioner-appellant separated his jama in respect of the land which he purchased from the opposite party Nos. 5 and 6 in the year 1992 and lost his right of pre-emption of the case land. Exhibit Gha, Mutation Register, clearly shows that mutation was approved in his name in respect of 0.0833 acre of land appertaining to the pre-emption petition schedule Ka land under the signature of Assistant Commissioner (Land) on 28-6-1993 vide Mutation Case No. 1354/92-93 DCR book of the year 1992/1993 (Exhibit Cha) shows that mutation fees and other fees amounting to Taka 28.50 were realised from him in connection with mutation case No.1354/92/-93 wherein a separate Khatian being No. 8399 with a jama of Taka 55.76 was opened anew in his name on 13-6-1993. Exhibit Chha, Rent Receipt Book, shows that land development tax ranging from 1396 BS to 1401 BS amounting to Taka 1163.50 paisa was realised from him on 23-1-1995 in respect of the said mutated Khatian being No.8399. Rent Collection Registers (Exhibit Uma, Uma (1) also carried particulars of such collection. By placing reliance on the said documents the learned Judge found that the petitioner-appellant, indeed, got his name mutated in 1993 in respect of the land which he purchased out of the case jote in the year of 1992 and already ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land when it was sold to the pre-emptee respondent No.1 in 1994. The aforesaid entries found place in those registers and receipt books in the usual course of business carried out by the public functionaries in the regular discharge of their duties. They have, therefore, presumptive value unless rebutted. The petitioner- appellant could not furnish any cogent evidence rebutting the same. Learned Judge rightly found that the petitioner-appellant had the opportunity to challenge the mutation proceeding to be a collusive and fictitious one by citing any of the co-sharers as a witness to prove that no notice was issued upon any of them in respect of mutation case No.1354/92-93 wherein his name was shown to have been mutated in respect of the land he purchased out of the case jote in 1992. But he refrained, which was quite meaningful. The learned Judge who closely scrutinised those registers and receipt books expressed with a profound belief that he found them to be genuine documents. There was thus overwhelming evidence on record showing a mutation case being No 13454/1992-1993 to have been legally started and completed at his instance opening a new Khatian bearing No. 8399 with a jama Taka 55.76 in his name on 13-6-1993 in respect of the land he purchased in 1992. It was not, therefore, much worthy of consideration if the mutation proceeding case record did not come before the court below on account of the circumstances, mention of which we have made earlier. The learned Judge thus rightly held that the petitioner having ceased to be a co-sharer in the case land he had no locus standi to claim pre-emption under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act.

15. We do not find any illegality to have been committed by the learned Judge in disallowing the pre-emption petition. It does not call for any interference by this court in its revisional jurisdiction.

16. In the result, the appeal is dismissed with costs. The impugned judgment and order dated 28- 2-2001 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Rangpur in Miscellaneous Case No. 25 of 1995 (a proceedings under section 24 of the Non-Agricultural Tenancy Act) disallowing pre-emption is hereby upheld.

Connected Rule No. 384 (FM) 2002 is discharged accordingly. Communicate the order to the court below at once. Send down the lower court records along with a copy of this judgment expeditiously.

End.
